newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Hanson gets ovation as Australian race row rolls on.
newsitem.headline: Hanson gets ovation as Australian race row rolls on.

text.p: The maverick politician at the centre of Australia's race row on Friday again called for a end to Asian immigration and dismissed government warnings she might harm the country's trade relations with its neighbours.

Populist independent Pauline Hanson received a standing ovation from conservative supporters in Queensland state after a 45-minute speech in which she repeated her call for an immediate end to immigration.
Hanson said immigration should be stopped immediately and when resumed it should only replace those who leave Australia permanently and only by those with a "basic fluency" in English.
"I believe you look after your own children before you look after your neighbour's kids," Hanson told a National Party meeting attended by around 170 fans.

Hanson's maiden parliamentary speech early last month, in which she said that Australia risked being swamped by Asians, sparked a national debate on race and immigration that has dogged mainstream political parties ever since.
Hanson has also complained that Aborigines -- Australia's most disadvantaged group -- get unfair preferential treament from the government.

Polls have shown that as many as seven out of 10 voters agree with Hanson that immigration is too high, although they do not necessarily endorse her politics. Australia accepted almost 100,000 immigrants last year, around a quarter of them Asians.
"I believe in one people, one nation, one flag. I believe in Pauline Hanson," one unidentified woman attending Hanson's meeting told Australian Broadcasting Corporation radio.
"We fought a war so that we could be free and we have virtually given it away to outsiders. We have lost our Australian identity," said another woman.
Hanson dismissed warnings about possible ill effects on Australian trade. "Our exports will continue to sell if the price is right," said Hanson.
Prime Minister John Howard has repeatedly refused to explicitly condemn Hanson's remarks, except to say that his government has no intention of ending its policy of non-discriminatory immigration.

In a radio interview on Thursday, Howard defended Australia as a tolerant society, despite its history of discrimination against Aborigines and its "White Australia" discriminatory immigration policy which ended in the early 1970s.
Historians say European settlers wiped out tens of thousands of Aborigines in the 18th and 19th centuries, sometimes in deliberate campaigns of extermination.

Trying to limit any economic damage, national immigration minister Philip Ruddock told a tourism seminar in Sydney that Australia's cultural diversity was a key component of its attraction as a tourist destination.
"The comments of some people have not been helpful," Ruddock said. "But as the prime minister said yesterday, most players in the region understand that those are not the views of the government."
